title: The Laws of Thermodynamics
summary: The first law is energy conservation for heat and work: $\Delta U=Q-W$. The second law says heat flows spontaneously hot → cold and no engine is perfectly efficient. Engine efficiency is bounded by the Carnot limit $1-T_c/T_h$.

internal energy.plain: Total microscopic energy of a system.
internal energy.in_class: Changes via heat and work: $\Delta U=Q-W$.

first law.plain: Energy conservation with heat and work.

work by a gas.plain: Work done as a gas expands.

second law.plain: Heat won't flow cold → hot on its own; entropy tends to increase.

heat engine.plain: A device converting heat to work.

efficiency.plain: Fraction of heat turned into work.

concept_sections.heading: The first law
concept_sections.explanation: Energy is conserved: the change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system, $\Delta U=Q-W$. Track signs carefully.
math_steps: Identify heat in $Q$ and work out $W$.
Positive $Q$ adds energy; positive $W$ removes it.

concept_sections.heading: Work in thermodynamic processes
concept_sections.explanation: A gas does work $W=\int P\,dV$ as it expands — the area under the $P$–$V$ curve. Constant-pressure work is $W=P\Delta V$.
math_steps: Work is the area under it.

concept_sections.heading: The second law
concept_sections.explanation: Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse without work, and entropy tends to increase. No process can convert heat entirely into work.
math_steps: Entropy of an isolated system increases.

concept_sections.heading: Heat engines and efficiency
concept_sections.explanation: An engine takes in $Q_h$, does work $W$, and dumps $Q_c$: efficiency $e=W/Q_h=1-Q_c/Q_h$. Real engines are well below the ideal.

concept_sections.heading: The Carnot limit
concept_sections.explanation: The maximum efficiency between reservoirs at $T_h$ and $T_c$ (kelvin) is $e_{max}=1-T_c/T_h$. No engine can beat it.

real_world_examples.title: A car engine
real_world_examples.scenario: Fuel burns to drive the car.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Only a fraction of the heat becomes work; the Carnot limit caps how good it can be.

real_world_examples.title: A refrigerator
real_world_examples.scenario: Heat is moved from cold to hot.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: This requires work input — the second law forbids it happening for free.

real_world_examples.title: Steam power plants
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Higher $T_h$ raises the Carnot efficiency, so plants run as hot as materials allow.

An engine takes $1000$ J and exhausts $600$ J. Find its efficiency.
Find the Carnot efficiency between $600$ K and $300$ K.
An engine does $400$ J of work per cycle taking in $1000$ J. Find the heat exhausted.
A gas releases $300$ J of heat while $150$ J of work is done on it. Find $\Delta U$.
